extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners and litigators (especially in pharmaceutical/biotech) drafting, defending, or challenging method-of-use and genus claims
extracted.subtask_description: Legal standards and practical criteria for written description and enablement of method-of-use (use-limited) patents in the life sciences, focusing on how genus disclosure, background knowledge, claim scope, and supporting evidence affect validity. Targets drafting, litigation, and prosecution strategy for therapeutics/antibody claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description: inventor must show 'possession' as of filing
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must demonstrate that the inventor was 'in possession' of the claimed invention as of the filing date; a genus can be disclosed either by a representative number of species or by structural features common to the genus so a skilled person can 'visualize or recognize' members of the genus (Ariad standard).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In life sciences, this is demanding where genera encompass vast numbers of compounds. Case examples include AbbVie (invalidated despite >300 antibodies) and Juno (invalidated with two embodiments). Use the Ariad two-prong approach when evaluating whether the specification shows possession. If the specification lacks representative species or common structural features, written-description support is at risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus disclosure can be supplemented by background knowledge when genus is well-known
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a genus is 'already well explored' and techniques for producing the relevant functionality are 'well known,' the specification can be read in light of the background knowledge in the art to find a representative number of species—particularly where the well-known techniques are not the core invention (Ajinomoto / In re Herschler / In re Fuetterer principle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply when the claimed invention is the use of a known genus rather than the genus itself. Courts will consider prior-art disclosures and common general knowledge to supply the missing species/teachings. Key conditions: (1) genus well explored in the art; (2) techniques to produce the claimed functionality are well known and routine; (3) those techniques are not the inventive aspect. Cite supportive precedent (Ajinomoto, Herschler, Fuetterer, Erfindergemeinschaft).

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative example + routine methods may suffice to show entire genus possession
rubrics_metrics.description: A single representative example (e.g., one humanized antibody 'G1'), together with disclosure of related nonhuman examples and explicit reference to routine methods (e.g., humanization techniques), can permit a finding that the inventor possessed the entire genus of humanized antibodies for the claimed use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teva accepted that one humanized example plus murine antibodies and an explicit statement that 'anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies may be made by any method known in the art' could demonstrate possession of the genus when humanization was routine and prior art provided extensive antibody disclosures. When relying on this approach, include: (a) at least one representative species; (b) disclosure or citation of routine methods to obtain other members; and (c) evidence that the genus/techniques were well-known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement: teach making and using the full claimed scope without undue experimentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must teach persons of ordinary skill how to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention without undue experimentation, and enablement must be commensurate with the scope of the claim (Amgen principle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For genus claims this usually requires sufficient guidance to make and use the entire class. Where making or screening members would require extensive time, effort, or expense (undue experimentation), enablement may fail (see Amgen, Baxalta, Idenix). Evaluate the quantity and quality of examples, protocols, and predictive guidance in the specification against the likely burden on a skilled artisan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim scope (functional/use-limited vs. full-genus-for-any-purpose) affects enablement rigor
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to a specific therapeutic use (method-of-use) are narrower in functional scope than claims that claim an entire genus for any and all purposes; narrower functional limits can reduce the enablement burden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teva distinguishes method-of-use claims (only humanized anti-CGRP antibodies to treat headache) from broad composition claims covering an entire genus for all uses. If the claimed function is limited and evidence indicates all members of the genus achieve that function, a practitioner may not need to enable making every genus member for every purpose. When drafting, emphasize functional limits to reduce enablement exposure; when litigating, argue (or challenge) whether the functional limitation truly narrows the inventive scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence that all genus members perform the claimed function
rubrics_metrics.description: Enablement/written-description support can be met if specification data and testimony permit a reasonable factfinder to conclude that all members of the claimed genus perform the claimed therapeutic function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will look to experimental data in the specification, expert testimony, prior-art teachings, and admissions (including opposing party statements in IPR/prosecution) to determine whether a skilled artisan would understand the entire genus is effective for the claimed use. Absent such evidence, enablement and possession may fail; affirmative experimental showing in the spec strengthens validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: no disclosed compounds or lack of knowledge in the art undermines written description
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patent discloses no compounds that could be used in the claimed methods and there is no evidence such compounds were known, written-description support is weak or absent (University of Rochester / Ariad caution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid claiming methods that require compounds not illustrated or otherwise supported by the specification or the common general knowledge. If the specification provides no enabling examples or the art does not establish that such compounds were known, courts have invalidated claims for lack of written description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine/established techniques cited in specification help both written description and enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly stating that members 'may be made by any method known in the art' and citing established prior-art methods for producing the claimed compounds can support both possession and enablement when those techniques are routine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft specifications to reference routine methods and include procedural detail or citations to standard protocols. The court in Teva relied on explicit disclosure of humanization methods and the routine nature of humanization; where techniques are truly routine, less experimental work may be required to practice the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution/record evidence (admissions, IPR arguments) can influence written-description/enablement analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements made by parties during IPR/prosecution/litigation (including arguments about what was known in the art) may be considered by courts and can bolster or undermine written-description and enablement findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Teva, Lilly's prior IPR arguments (that humanized antibodies were not known) were used against it because the court found the record supported that humanization was routine and the art was replete with relevant disclosures. Be mindful that adversarial admissions and prior procedural positions can be used as evidence; coordinate prosecution and litigation positions to avoid detrimental concessions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical drafting and litigation strategy for life-sciences method-of-use/genus claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners should tailor claim drafting, specification disclosure, and litigation arguments to the framework distinguishing novel genera from uses of well-known genera — e.g., emphasize use-limited claims, include representative examples and data, disclose routine methods, and document the state of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drafting: (a) include at least one representative example with data; (b) disclose routine methods and cite prior art; (c) consider claiming the method/use rather than the full genus for broad protection while reducing enablement risk. When defending: marshal specification data, expert testimony, and prior-art evidence showing genus well-known and techniques routine. When attacking: show insufficiency of representative examples, lack of background knowledge, or undue experimentation required to practice full scope.
